new_statements.rule_in_words: Momuna is described as a tone language: monosyllables contrast three tone levels (high, mid, low); polysyllabic words contrast only two levels, and that contrast is carried by the word's stressed syllable alone. The note presupposes one stressed syllable per polysyllabic word but gives no rule for its position (initial, final, weight-based or lexical) and no statement on predictability. Usher's New Guinea World summary of the same and of Reimer's unpublished phonology restates it as tone 'on the vowel which carries primary stress' and adds that Reimer's texts nonetheless mark high and low tones on disyllables without explanation.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the passage is a phoneme/orthography footnote in a discourse paper, not a phonology.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (monosyllabic vs non-monosyllabic words) in the orthographic transcription used for the texts; Reimer's data are from Sumo village on the Balim (Vriendschap) River, i.e. the Balim River dialect. Stress placement itself is unstated, so no positional reading can be assigned; the system as described (tone contrast confined to the stressed syllable) is compatible with a culminative pitch-accent analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Reimer's data are Momuna of Sumo village on the Balim (Vriendschap) River, i.e. the Balim River dialect of Momuna [mqf] = momu1241. 'Momina' [mmb] (momi1242, Glottolog 5.1 sister in Somahai) is per current Glottolog a spurious duplicate of Momuna (Rekai River dialect pronunciation, Kroneman & Peckham 1989 misread; Wälchli 2025:433 knows no documentation of a separate Momina); the same Reimer 1986 statement was already filed under momi1242 in this audit and belongs here.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. Momuna. New Guinea World (Santa Fe Institute), page last modified 2024-06-25.
sources.note: Second-hand from Reimer 1986 and an unpublished Reimer (n.d.) phonology: 'According to Reimer, three tones, high mid and low, are distinguished in monosyllables. In words with more than one syllable, two tones are distinguished on the vowel which carries primary stress. However, Reimer's materials still mark both high and low tones, along with unmarked mid tones, on disyllables without explanation.' No placement rule. Lists further Reimer items (1990 texts, 1991 vocabulary, n.d. phonology) not available online.
